subject: mathematics
question_text: Find the inverse of the matrix A with rows (2, 1, 2), (1, 0, 1) and (2, 2, 1).

mark_split.label: Find det A and check it is not zero
Transpose to Adj A and divide by det A

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.53 — SAQ chapter 7 Matrices, answer 42.2. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag. THE 1+2+1 SPLIT IS EFFECTIVELY THE BOOK'S, by a route worth stating: the book asserts on book p.30 that "Just finding A⁻¹ gives u 4 Marks", and this SAQ asks for exactly that and is worth exactly 4 marks — so the whole question IS the book's own 4-mark chunk. The division of that chunk into 1 (determinant) + 2 (nine cofactors) + 1 (transpose and divide) is OURS, and is the same division the matrix-inversion LAQs in this unit use. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all four "find the inverse" SAQs in this unit, deliberately: they are one method over different numbers. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads "4 Marks"; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q11 is the Matrices slot.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the inverse of this matrix — name each thing you have to work out, in order.

steps.label: Find det A
steps.margin_note: First mark. det A comes to 1. Row 2 has a 0 in it, so expanding along the top row and using that zero keeps the arithmetic short.
steps.memory_tip: det A = 1. Row 2 has a 0, so expanding along the top row and using it keeps the arithmetic short.
lines: det A = 1 ≠ 0, so A is non-singular and A⁻¹ exists.

recall.must_convey: That det A is computed, comes to 1, and that being non-zero is what guarantees A⁻¹ exists.
accept: find the determinant of A which is 1 and it is not zero so the inverse exists
compute det A and check it is non zero so A is non singular
expand the determinant, it is not zero so A inverse exists
det A kanukoni, zero kaadu kabatti inverse untundi
the determinant must be non zero for the inverse to exist

steps.why: A⁻¹ is the adjoint divided by det A. A zero determinant would mean dividing by zero, which is exactly why a singular matrix has no inverse — so this line is a gate, not a warm-up.
common_mistakes: Computing det A but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong: plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Starting the cofactors before checking the determinant.

steps.label: Find the cofactor matrix
steps.margin_note: Half the marks, and nine small determinants. Delete the entry’s own row and column, take the 2×2 determinant of what is left, then apply the sign board + − + / − + − / + − +. Work along the rows in order so none is missed.
steps.memory_tip: Nine small determinants with the sign board applied after each.
lines: Delete each entry’s row and column, take the 2×2

recall.must_convey: That each cofactor is the 2×2 determinant left after deleting that entry’s row and column, with the alternating sign applied.
accept: for each entry delete its row and column take the two by two determinant and apply the plus minus sign
find the nine cofactors from the minors with the alternating sign pattern
cross out the row and column of each entry and take the determinant of what is left with the right sign
prathi entry ki row column teesesi two by two determinant teeskoni sign pettali
build the cofactor matrix from the nine minors with signs plus minus plus

steps.why: A minor is the smaller determinant; a cofactor is that minor with a sign attached, and the sign depends only on the position. That is why the board is worth learning once instead of re-deriving nine times.
common_mistakes: Writing the minors and forgetting the sign board entirely.
Applying the signs to the wrong positions; all four corners are plus.
Deleting the wrong row or column for the off-diagonal entries.

steps.label: Transpose and divide
steps.margin_note: Last mark. det A is 1, so A⁻¹ is the adjoint unchanged. Still write the division line: the method is what is being marked, and the next question will not be so kind.
steps.memory_tip: det A is 1, so A⁻¹ is the adjoint unchanged — but still write the division line.
lines: Adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix:

recall.must_convey: That the adjoint is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix, and that A⁻¹ is that adjoint divided by det A.
accept: take the transpose of the cofactor matrix to get adj A then divide by det A
adjoint is the transpose of the cofactors and A inverse is adj A over det A
transpose the cofactor matrix and divide every entry by the determinant
cofactor matrix transpose teeste adj A, det A tho divide cheste inverse
A inverse equals one by det A times the adjoint

steps.why: Skipping the transpose gives a matrix that looks right and is wrong, and nothing in the question will reveal it. Writing the word "transpose" on the page is the habit that prevents it.
common_mistakes: Using the cofactor matrix directly as the adjoint without transposing.
Dividing only one row by det A instead of every entry.
Multiplying by det A instead of dividing.
